title: Oil Tumbled 3% on the Israel-Lebanon Ceasefire. India Is Watching for the Hormuz Breakthrough That Has Not Come.
excerpt: Brent fell to $95 as markets bet on a broader Iran deal. For India, the question is whether this ceasefire holds long enough to reopen the strait that carried 40 percent of its crude.
body:
Oil prices fell sharply on Thursday after Israel and Lebanon announced a ceasefire agreement, raising the first serious hopes in months that a broader deal to end the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran could be within reach — and that the Strait of Hormuz, the most important chokepoint in global energy, might eventually reopen.

Brent crude dropped as much as $2.62, or 2.7 percent, to $95.19 a barrel. West Texas Intermediate fell $3.27, or 3.4 percent, to $92.75. Both benchmarks had risen about 2 percent the previous day after renewed hostilities, including Iranian strikes on Kuwait's airport and U.S. military strikes near the Strait of Hormuz.

The significance for India is immediate and material. The strait, through which more than 40 percent of India's crude oil imports flowed before the war began, has been largely closed for more than three months. The disruption has forced the world's third-largest oil importer into a frantic diversification effort — turning to Venezuela, whose interim President Delcy Rodriguez was in Delhi on Thursday for energy talks, and leaning harder on African and Russian suppliers.

The ceasefire itself is conditional. Under the U.S.-brokered agreement, Hezbollah would withdraw its fighters from southern Lebanon and halt attacks on Israel, while the Lebanese Armed Forces would take exclusive control of the territory. Lebanese President Joseph Aoun said Thursday that the ceasefire would come into force within 24 hours of all concerned parties approving it — an implicit reference to Hezbollah, which has not yet commented on the deal.

But the reason oil markets moved is not the Lebanon deal itself. It is what the Lebanon deal might unlock. Tehran has made a ceasefire in Lebanon an explicit condition for any peace deal with Washington. If Hezbollah stands down, one of Iran's central demands is met, and the diplomatic path to a broader agreement — one that could reopen the strait — becomes marginally less impossible.

U.S. President Donald Trump suggested Wednesday that there could be progress in negotiations with Iran "as soon as this weekend." Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi was more measured, saying Tehran's contacts with Washington had not been cut off but that no meaningful progress had been made. Both sides, he said, were studying texts that had been exchanged.

The skepticism is warranted. A previous U.S.-brokered ceasefire in April failed within days. Israel's Defence Minister Israel Katz said Thursday that the military would continue to strike in Lebanon for the time being and would not withdraw from the south. Hezbollah's chief Naim Qassem said that as long as Lebanese villages were being bombed, northern Israel would not be safe.

For Indian policymakers, the oil price dip offers a moment of relief but not a solution. The Reserve Bank of India is widely expected to hold its key rate at 5.25 percent on Friday, but the policy direction is shifting. War-fuelled inflation has pushed shorter-duration bond yields higher, and foreign investors have responded by piling into short-term Indian government bonds — a bet that a rate hike is coming, even if not immediately.

The Indian economy has absorbed the energy shock better than many predicted, in part because the government moved quickly to diversify supply and because strategic petroleum reserves provided a cushion. But the cushion is thinning. U.S. commercial crude stocks fell by 8 million barrels last week, with an additional 8 million released from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. Global inventories are tightening into the third quarter.

"Without a normalisation of regional oil flows, the market is increasingly exposed to sharp upward swings as inventories continue to thin," analysts at ING wrote Thursday.

The Israel-Lebanon ceasefire is a necessary step toward peace, but it is not a sufficient one. For India, the question that matters most — when the Strait of Hormuz reopens — remains unanswered. Thursday's oil price drop is a wager that the answer is closer than it was yesterday. The market has made that bet before, and lost.

*Sources: Reuters, OilPrice.com, Wall Street Journal*
